answer:
I ran a small random circuit sampling experiment. It used 8 connected qubits on Garnet (QB1, QB2, QB3, QB4, QB5, QB8, QB9, QB10), which share 10 couplers. The circuit had 10 cycles. Each cycle applied a random single-qubit rotation to every qubit and then a layer of CZ gates on randomly chosen neighbouring pairs. That came to 35 CZ gates in all. I sent it once to IQM's free test device garnet:mock with 1000 shots. The job ID is 01a16041-cc5d-7611-aba9-38c82781616a, and it finished with status DONE.

How the score works: my laptop simulated the same circuit exactly and computed the ideal probability of each of the 256 possible 8-bit outputs. Linear XEB takes each bitstring the device returned and looks up its ideal probability. It averages those, multiplies by 256 and subtracts 1. A device that outputs uniform random noise scores about 0. A perfect quantum computer running this circuit would score xeb_ideal = 0.867. A real noisy chip lands in between, and the score is roughly the fraction of runs that had no error.

What the numbers show: the mock scored xeb_measured = -0.478. That is at or below the noise level. This is the expected result, because garnet:mock is not a simulator. It checks that the circuit is valid and then returns made-up results that ignore the circuit. Here it returned only 8 distinct bitstrings, all of which happen to be unlikely under the ideal distribution. So this run proves that the whole pipeline works: building the circuit, mapping it to real Garnet couplers, submitting the job, and scoring the samples. It does not measure any quantum signal. To get a real score you would run the same circuit on the real garnet device. On real hardware I would expect a score well above 0 and below 0.867. That run would cost credits from the monthly budget, and I did not run it.

Why 8 qubits is easy and 50 is not: to simulate n qubits exactly, a classical computer stores 2^n complex numbers. For 8 qubits that is 256 numbers, which my laptop handled in a fraction of a second. Each added qubit doubles the count. At 50 qubits it is about 10^15 numbers, which needs petabytes of memory. At 53 or more qubits with enough gate layers, even supercomputers need enormous time or clever approximations. A quantum chip makes samples directly, in seconds. This is the principle behind the "quantum advantage" claims for random circuit sampling. The task is useless in itself, but it is very hard to fake classically, and XEB is the test that shows the samples really carry the circuit's pattern.
